song-dynasty.name: Song dynasty
song-dynasty.summary: Imperial Chinese dynasty that ruled from 960 to 1279, later split into a northern and southern period after losing northern China to the Jurchen Jin dynasty, before its conquest by the Mongols.

tang-dynasty.name: Tang dynasty
tang-dynasty.summary: Chinese imperial dynasty that ruled from 618 to 907, with an interruption from 690 to 705, widely regarded as a golden age of cosmopolitan Chinese civilisation.

yuan-dynasty.name: Yuan dynasty
yuan-dynasty.summary: A Mongol-led dynasty ruling China from 1271 to 1368, founded by Kublai Khan, and the first non-Han dynasty to rule all of China.

hu-sihui.name: Hu Sihui
hu-sihui.summary: Chinese court therapist and dietitian under the Yuan dynasty, active around 1314–1330, known for his book on dietary principles and for describing deficiency diseases.

yinshan-zhengyao.name: Yinshan Zhengyao
yinshan-zhengyao.summary: Chinese cookbook and medical text written by Hu Sihui, first published in 1330; surviving editions descend from a 1456 Ming dynasty printing.

bai-people.name: Bai people
bai-people.summary: An East Asian ethnic group native to Yunnan, Guizhou and Hunan provinces in China, one of the country's 56 officially recognized ethnic groups.

jayaatu-khan-tugh-tem-r.name: Tugh Temür
jayaatu-khan-tugh-tem-r.summary: A Yuan dynasty emperor (1304–1332), also known as Jayaatu Khan or Emperor Wenzong, who ruled twice between 1328 and 1332 and sponsored poetry, painting and a major compilation of Yuan governance practices.

columbian-exchange.name: Columbian exchange
columbian-exchange.summary: The widespread transfer of plants, animals and diseases between the Americas and Afro-Eurasia beginning in the late 15th century, named for Christopher Columbus.

ming-dynasty.name: Ming dynasty
ming-dynasty.summary: China's last dynasty ruled by the Han majority, reigning 1368 to 1644 after the Mongol-led Yuan dynasty's fall, founded by the Hongwu Emperor.

huang-gongwang.name: Huang Gongwang
huang-gongwang.summary: Chinese painter, poet and writer (1269–1354) born at the end of the Song dynasty, considered the eldest of the 'Four Masters of the Yuan dynasty'.

yingzao-fashi.name: Yingzao Fashi
yingzao-fashi.summary: Chinese treatise on architecture and craftsmanship, written by Li Jie and published in 1103, setting building standards for architects and government agencies.

li-jie-song-dynasty.name: Li Jie
li-jie-song-dynasty.summary: Chinese architect and writer of the Northern Song dynasty (1065–1110) who wrote the Yingzao Fashi, a technical treatise on architecture and craftsmanship.

ni-zan.name: Ni Zan
ni-zan.summary: Chinese painter (1301–1374) of the Yuan and early Ming periods, counted among the Four Masters of the Yuan dynasty alongside Huang Gongwang, Wu Zhen and Wang Meng.

qing-dynasty.name: Qing dynasty
qing-dynasty.summary: Manchu-led imperial dynasty of China from 1644 to 1912, the last imperial dynasty, which at its height controlled more territory than any other dynasty in Chinese history.

weifang.name: Weifang
weifang.summary: Prefecture-level city in central Shandong province, China, known for historic sites and traditional New Year woodcuts, with a population of over 9 million.

chinese-knotting.name: Chinese knotting
chinese-knotting.summary: A folk art of weaving a single cord into symbolic shapes, tied to Buddhism and Taoism; once used to record information before writing was common, and later worn as good-luck charms.

liao-dynasty.name: Liao dynasty
liao-dynasty.summary: A Khitan-led imperial dynasty of China (916–1125) that at its height ruled Manchuria, Mongolia, northern Korea, and parts of Siberia and North China.

jin-dynasty-1115-1234.name: Jin dynasty
jin-dynasty-1115-1234.summary: Jurchen-led dynasty of China (1115–1234) that overthrew the Liao, fought a century-long war with the Song, and was eventually conquered by the Mongols.

kaifeng.name: Kaifeng
kaifeng.summary: City in Henan, China, formerly called Bianjing, that served as capital of the Northern Song dynasty until it was sacked in 1127.

jingkang-incident.name: Jingkang Incident
jingkang-incident.summary: 1127 sack of the Song capital Bianjing by Jin forces, who captured the emperor and his family, ending the Northern Song dynasty.

western-xia.name: Western Xia
western-xia.summary: A Tangut-led dynasty ruling north-central China from 1038 to 1227, controlling part of the Silk Road until it was destroyed by the Mongols.

jin-song-wars.name: Jin-Song Wars
jin-song-wars.summary: Series of conflicts beginning in 1125 in which the Jurchen Jin dynasty invaded the Song, culminating in the capture of the Song emperor and loss of northern China.

i-vi-t.name: Đại Việt
i-vi-t.summary: The official name of several Vietnamese monarchies centered on modern Hanoi, first adopted as Đại Cồ Việt in 968 by Emperor Đinh Bộ Lĩnh. It lasted, mostly as Đại Việt, until 1804, when it was renamed Việt Nam.

hanoi.name: Thăng Long (Hanoi)
hanoi.summary: The name given to Hanoi when Emperor Lý Thái Tổ founded it as capital of Đại Việt in 1010; the city was later renamed Hanoi in 1831.

qara-khitai.name: Qara Khitai
qara-khitai.summary: A dynastic state founded in Central Asia by Khitans displaced after the fall of the Liao dynasty, governing a mostly Turkic and Iranian population until conquered by the Mongols in 1218.

hongwu-emperor.name: Hongwu Emperor (Zhu Yuanzhang)
hongwu-emperor.summary: Founding emperor of the Ming dynasty (1328 to 1398) who rose from a peasant family, joined the Red Turban rebels, and drove out Mongol Yuan rule to reunify China.

mongol-invasions-of-japan.name: Mongol invasions of Japan
mongol-invasions-of-japan.summary: Two failed attempts by Kublai Khan's Yuan dynasty to conquer Japan, in 1274 and 1281, remembered as the origin of the word kamikaze, or divine wind, for the typhoons that wrecked the invasion fleets.

han-dynasty.name: Han dynasty
han-dynasty.summary: An imperial Chinese dynasty (202 BC–220 AD) seen as a golden age of Chinese history; the majority Chinese ethnic group, language and script are named after it.

ci-poetry.name: Ci (poetry)
ci-poetry.summary: A form of Classical Chinese lyric poetry with lines of irregular length set to fixed musical patterns, which flourished under the Song and Yuan dynasties.

bi-sheng.name: Bi Sheng
bi-sheng.summary: A Chinese artisan of the Song dynasty, died 1051, who invented the world's first movable type between 1039 and 1048 using fired clay tiles for each character.

movable-type.name: Movable type
movable-type.summary: A printing technology using individual, reusable characters to compose text, rather than carving whole pages as blocks.

woodblock-printing.name: Woodblock printing
woodblock-printing.summary: A relief printing technique using carved wooden blocks, originating in China in antiquity and used across East Asia for texts and images until the 19th century.

ouyang-xiu.name: Ouyang Xiu
ouyang-xiu.summary: A Song dynasty historian, poet, essayist and politician (1007–1072) considered the central figure of the Eight Masters of Tang and Song prose, who compiled the New Book of Tang and backed the 1040s Qingli Reforms.

su-shi.name: Su Shi
su-shi.summary: Song dynasty scholar-official, poet, calligrapher and painter (1037–1101) whose prolific, influential work flourished during repeated periods of political exile.

wang-anshi.name: Wang Anshi
wang-anshi.summary: A Chinese politician, poet and philosopher (1021–1086) of the Song dynasty who served as chancellor and pushed through sweeping, controversial economic and military reforms known as the New Policies.

sanqu.name: Sanqu
sanqu.summary: A fixed-rhythm form of Classical Chinese poetry, or 'literary song,' associated especially with the Yuan, Ming and Qing dynasties, based on folk tunes.

sima-guang.name: Sima Guang
sima-guang.summary: Chinese historian and Song dynasty official, 1019–1086, who wrote the monumental Zizhi Tongjian and opposed Wang Anshi's reform policies.

zizhi-tongjian.name: Zizhi Tongjian
zizhi-tongjian.summary: A Chinese historical chronicle presented in 1084, covering 403 BC to 959 AD across 16 dynasties, compiled over 19 years by official Sima Guang (1019-1086).

emperor-shenzong-of-song.name: Emperor Shenzong of Song
emperor-shenzong-of-song.summary: Sixth emperor of China's Song dynasty (1048–1085), known for backing Wang Anshi's New Policies and for actively pursuing territorial expansion and fiscal reform.

classic-of-poetry.name: Classic of Poetry
classic-of-poetry.summary: The oldest surviving collection of Chinese poetry, comprising 305 works from the 11th to 7th centuries BC and traditionally said to be edited by Confucius.

sakya-pandita.name: Sakya Pandita
sakya-pandita.summary: Tibetan spiritual leader and Buddhist scholar (1182 to 1251), the fourth of the Five Sakya Forefathers, renowned for mastery of Sanskrit and the major and minor sciences.

odoric-of-pordenone.name: Odoric of Pordenone
odoric-of-pordenone.summary: A Franciscan friar and missionary explorer (c. 1280–1331) who traveled through India, Southeast Asia and China before returning to write an influential account of the Far East.

hangzhou.name: Hangzhou
hangzhou.summary: A city in eastern China that served as capital of the Wuyue Kingdom and later the Southern Song dynasty, renowned for its West Lake.

zhangzhou.name: Zhangzhou
zhangzhou.summary: A prefecture-level city in Fujian Province, China, on the Taiwan Strait near Xiamen, visited by the medieval Franciscan friar Odoric of Pordenone.

su-song.name: Su Song
su-song.summary: Song dynasty polymath (1020–1101) skilled in astronomy, mechanics and more, who engineered a hydro-mechanical clock tower with an early escapement and the earliest known chain drive.

escapement.name: Escapement
escapement.summary: A mechanical linkage in clocks and watches that regulates the gear train's advance and produces the timepiece's characteristic ticking; first invented in 13th-century Europe.

chain-drive.name: Chain drive
chain-drive.summary: A way of transmitting mechanical power by a chain running over toothed gears, commonly used in bicycles and motorcycles as well as many other machines.

armillary-sphere.name: Armillary sphere
armillary-sphere.summary: Model of the celestial sphere made of rings representing lines such as the ecliptic, invented separately in ancient China and Greece and later used in the Islamic world and medieval Europe.

roger-bacon.name: Roger Bacon
roger-bacon.summary: Roger Bacon: Medieval English polymath, philosopher and Franciscan friar (c. 1219–c. 1292) who emphasized empirical study of nature and is considered one of the earliest European advocates of the modern scientific method.

opus-majus.name: Opus Majus
opus-majus.summary: Roger Bacon's 878-page treatise, written in 1267 for Pope Clement IV, covering grammar, logic, mathematics, physics and philosophy; two shorter companion works followed it that same year.

four-great-inventions.name: Four Great Inventions
four-great-inventions.summary: The compass, gunpowder, papermaking and printing—four Chinese inventions celebrated as symbols of ancient China's advanced technology.

imperial-examination.name: Imperial examination
imperial-examination.summary: Merit-based system for selecting Chinese state officials, formalized under the Tang and Song dynasties and lasting until its abolition in 1905.

jurchen-people.name: Jurchen
jurchen-people.summary: Tungusic-speaking peoples of northeastern China who founded the Jin and Qing dynasties; they were renamed Manchus in 1635 by Hong Taiji.

shen-kuo.name: Shen Kuo
shen-kuo.summary: Chinese polymath, scientist and statesman of the Northern Song dynasty (1031–1095), first to describe the magnetic needle compass in his 1088 essays.

hand-cannon.name: Hand cannon
hand-cannon.summary: The earliest true firearm, used in China from the 13th century and across Eurasia by the 14th, fired by manually lighting a touch hole.

patricia-buckley-ebrey.name: Patricia B. Ebrey
patricia-buckley-ebrey.summary: An American art historian and sinologist, born 1947, specializing in cultural and gender issues of China's Song Dynasty; professor emerita at the University of Washington.

hong-mai.name: Hong Mai
hong-mai.summary: Chinese statesman, Confucian scholar and writer of the Southern Song dynasty (1123 to 1202), author of Yijianzhi and Rongzhai Suibi.

kublai-khan.name: Kublai Khan
kublai-khan.summary: Founder and first emperor of the Mongol-led Yuan dynasty of China (r. 1260–1294), grandson of Genghis Khan, who completed the conquest of the Song by 1279.

battle-of-yamen.name: Battle of Yamen
battle-of-yamen.summary: A naval battle fought on 19 March 1279 in southern China, considered the last stand of the Song dynasty against the Mongol-led Yuan dynasty.

nanjing.name: Nanjing
nanjing.summary: A major city in eastern China that served as the capital of numerous Chinese dynasties, kingdoms and governments from the 3rd century to 1949.

oirats.name: Oirats
oirats.summary: The westernmost group of Mongols, originally from the Altai region of Siberia, Xinjiang and western Mongolia; today's Kalmyks of southeastern Europe descend from them.

esen-taishi.name: Esen Taishi
esen-taishi.summary: Oirat leader and khagan of the Northern Yuan dynasty (d. 1455) who unified Mongolia and captured a Ming emperor at the 1449 Battle of Tumu Fortress.

wang-zhen-eunuch.name: Wang Zhen
wang-zhen-eunuch.summary: Ming dynasty court eunuch who became the first eunuch to hold major political power, advising the boy Zhengtong Emperor, and was killed in the 1449 Tumu Crisis when the emperor was captured.

emperor-yingzong-of-ming.name: Zhengtong Emperor
emperor-yingzong-of-ming.summary: Era name of Emperor Yingzong of Ming's first reign (1435–1449), during which the Ming empire was at its height before he was captured by Mongol forces at the Battle of Tumu Fortress.

tumu-crisis.name: Tumu Crisis
tumu-crisis.summary: An 1449 border conflict in which Oirat Mongols crushingly defeated the Ming dynasty's army and captured its emperor, one of the biggest military failures in Ming history.

huang-ming-zuxun.name: Huang-Ming Zuxun
huang-ming-zuxun.summary: Ancestral instructions composed in 1373 by the Ming dynasty's founder, the Hongwu Emperor, to guide his descendants in governance, ritual and administration.

jianwen-emperor.name: Jianwen Emperor
jianwen-emperor.summary: Second emperor of China's Ming dynasty (1377–1402), reigning 1398 to 1402; his attempt to curb the power of his uncles triggered the Jingnan civil war, after which he disappeared and his uncle took the throne as the Yongle Emperor.

jingnan-campaign.name: Jingnan campaign
jingnan-campaign.summary: 1399–1402 civil war of the early Ming dynasty in which Zhu Di overthrew his nephew, the Jianwen Emperor, and took the throne as the Yongle Emperor.

yongle-emperor.name: Yongle Emperor
yongle-emperor.summary: Third emperor of the Ming dynasty, reigning 1402 to 1424 after seizing the throne from his nephew; moved the capital to Beijing and sponsored the Yongle Encyclopedia.

jingtai-emperor.name: Jingtai Emperor
jingtai-emperor.summary: Seventh Ming emperor (r. 1449–1457) who took the throne after his brother was captured by the Mongols, later overthrown in a coup that restored his brother.

yu-qian.name: Yu Qian
yu-qian.summary: A Ming dynasty official (1398–1457) who led Beijing's defense against the Mongols during the Tumu Crisis and became the government's most influential minister.

cai-jing.name: Cai Jing
cai-jing.summary: A Chinese calligrapher and politician of the Northern Song dynasty (1047 to 1126) who served as chancellor four times and is fictionalized as a villain in the novel Water Margin.

emperor-zhezong.name: Emperor Zhezong
emperor-zhezong.summary: Seventh emperor of the Song dynasty, reigning from 1085 until his death in 1100, who took the throne at age nine under his grandmother's regency.

new-policies-song-dynasty.name: New Policies
new-policies-song-dynasty.summary: A series of reforms launched by Northern Song dynasty minister Wang Anshi under Emperor Shenzong from 1069 to 1076, later repealed and reinstated repeatedly in court politics.

emperor-huizong-of-song.name: Emperor Huizong of Song
emperor-huizong-of-song.summary: Eighth emperor of China's Song dynasty (1082–1135), an accomplished painter, poet and calligrapher whose lavish rule ended when Jin forces captured him and the capital in 1127.

fang-la.name: Fang La
fang-la.summary: Chinese rebel leader who led an uprising against the Song dynasty, dying in 1121; later fictionalised as a villain in the novel Water Margin.

toghon-tem-r.name: Toghon Temür
toghon-tem-r.summary: Last emperor of the Yuan dynasty (r. 1333-1368), who retreated to the Mongolian steppe after Zhu Yuanzhang founded the Ming dynasty and captured Khanbaliq in 1368.

pope-benedict-xii.name: Pope Benedict XII
pope-benedict-xii.summary: Born Jacques Fournier, head of the Catholic Church from 1334 to 1342; reformed monastic orders and began the great papal palace at Avignon.

dadu-beijing.name: Khanbaliq
dadu-beijing.summary: The Mongol name, meaning 'the khan's city,' for Dadu, the winter capital of the Yuan dynasty on the site of modern Beijing, ruled by Kublai Khan and his successors.

giovanni-de-marignolli.name: Giovanni de' Marignolli
giovanni-de-marignolli.summary: A 14th-century Catholic traveller (active 1338–1353) who journeyed to medieval China and India, later serving as a papal legate to the Yuan court.

semu.name: Semu
semu.summary: A privileged class of foreign, mostly Central and East Asian officials under China's Yuan dynasty, one of four social tiers alongside the Mongols, Hanren and Nanren.

qadi.name: Qadi
qadi.summary: The magistrate or judge of a Sharia court, who also handled mediation, guardianship of orphans, and oversight of public works.

quanzhou.name: Quanzhou
quanzhou.summary: Major Chinese port city in Fujian province, visited by Marco Polo and Ibn Battuta, a cosmopolitan medieval trading hub with temples, mosques and churches and a base for Mongol naval attacks on Japan and Java.

neo-confucianism.name: Neo-Confucianism
neo-confucianism.summary: A revival of Confucianism as an ethical, social and religious system that dominated Chinese philosophy from the 13th to 19th century, developed under Zhu Xi during the Song dynasty.

refuge-in-buddhism.name: Three Jewels
refuge-in-buddhism.summary: In Buddhism, the Three Jewels — the Buddha, the Dharma and the Sangha — that a follower takes refuge in as the core of a devoted life, common to all major Buddhist schools.

sui-dynasty.name: Sui dynasty
sui-dynasty.summary: Chinese imperial dynasty that ruled from 581 to 618 CE, reuniting China after centuries of division and laying groundwork for the following Tang dynasty's golden age.

zhu-xi.name: Zhu Xi
zhu-xi.summary: A Chinese philosopher, historian and politician (1130–1200) of the Southern Song dynasty, the leading figure of Neo-Confucianism, whose commentaries were core exam texts until 1905.

wang-yangming.name: Wang Yangming
wang-yangming.summary: Ming dynasty Chinese statesman, general and Neo-Confucian philosopher (1472–1529), regarded as the most important Neo-Confucian thinker after Zhu Xi and founder of the Lu–Wang school of thought.

joseon.name: Joseon
joseon.summary: A Korean dynastic kingdom founded in 1392 by Taejo, lasting 505 years until 1897, which entrenched Confucian ideals and saw the height of classical Korean culture and science.

lingbao-school.name: Lingbao School
lingbao-school.summary: A Daoist school that emerged in China in the early fifth century CE, blending Shangqing Daoist texts, Celestial Master rituals and Buddhist ideas like reincarnation, lasting about two hundred years.

quanzhen-school.name: Quanzhen School
quanzhen-school.summary: Taoist denomination founded in 1170 in Shandong that helped preserve Han Chinese lives during the Mongol invasion and remains one of China's largest Taoist sects today.

emperor-xingzong-of-liao.name: Emperor Xingzong of Liao
emperor-xingzong-of-liao.summary: Seventh emperor of the Khitan-led Liao dynasty of China, reigning from 1016 to 1055.

buddhist-canons.name: Tripitaka
buddhist-canons.summary: Traditional term meaning "Triple Basket" for the three main divisions of certain ancient Buddhist scriptural canons: monastic rules, teachings, and scholastic works.

manichaeism.name: Manichaeism
manichaeism.summary: A major dualistic religion founded in the 3rd century CE by the prophet Mani, teaching a cosmic struggle between light and darkness and drawing on Zoroastrian, Christian and Buddhist traditions.

jinshi.name: Jinshi
jinshi.summary: Highest and final degree awarded in Imperial China's civil service examinations, taken in the capital and also called the Metropolitan Exam.

chinese-classics.name: Confucian classics
chinese-classics.summary: Works of Chinese literature written before 221 BC, including the Four Books and Five Classics; mastering them in Classical Chinese was required for the imperial examinations that produced China's scholar-officials.

shiva.name: Shiva
shiva.summary: One of the principal deities of Hinduism, worshipped as the Supreme Being in Shaivism and known as 'the Destroyer' within the Hindu trinity alongside Brahma and Vishnu.

khitan-people.name: Khitan people
khitan-people.summary: A nomadic East Asian people descended from the Xianbei who founded the Liao dynasty (916–1125) ruling Mongolia, Siberia and northern China, and later the Qara Khitai in Central Asia; the name Cathay derives from theirs.

manigramam.name: Manigramam
manigramam.summary: A medieval merchant guild of itinerant Indian traders active mainly in southern India, operating in both port towns and inland trade centers alongside other major trading guilds.

kaiyuan-temple-quanzhou.name: Kaiyuan Temple
kaiyuan-temple-quanzhou.summary: A Buddhist temple in Quanzhou, China, the largest in Fujian province, notable for containing Hindu monuments left by traders from Southern India and for its role in medieval maritime trade.

john-of-montecorvino.name: John of Montecorvino
john-of-montecorvino.summary: Italian Franciscan missionary (1247–1328) who founded the earliest Latin Catholic missions in India and China and became Archbishop of Peking, converting many in Yuan-dynasty Beijing.
